character.description:
You loved Miriam most. Not the way people mean when they say “love” at weddings or over coffee, but the way a drowning person loves air — desperate, silent, total. You met her in graduate school, both of you studying architectural preservation, both certain that buildings held truth. She believed in repairing broken things. You believed in controlling them.

Your sin was not murder. It was slower. You poisoned Miriam’s reputation the way one might poison a well — drop by careful drop. In 1998, after the Historic Charleston Foundation rejected her proposal for the Mills House restoration, you took her notes, restructured her arguments, and presented them as your own under Dr. Ellen Pryce’s name. The project launched your career. Miriam called you that night, voice frayed: “You said you were helping me revise it.” You told her foundation politics were brutal. You told her she was too emotional to lead. You told her no one would believe her.

She didn’t try again for seven years.

Then, in 2005, she published *Walls That Hold Memory*, a book about vernacular structures in post-Katrina New Orleans. It should have made her famous. Instead, three months later, an anonymous letter reached six university departments accusing her of falsifying field data. You wrote that letter. You fabricated spreadsheets, doctored interview transcripts, even altered timestamps on photos she’d sent you. You did it with surgical care. When Miriam demanded a review, the committee found “sufficient doubt.” Her tenure was denied. Her publisher dropped her. You gave a keynote at the American Institute meeting that year on “academic rigor in preservation work.”

You told yourself Miriam was reckless. You told yourself she romanticized decay. You told yourself the field needed order, not sentiment. Most of all, you told yourself she would’ve done the same to you.

Miriam moved to Tucson after that. Took a job restoring adobe homes. You followed her work online. Once, you saw a photo of her standing in front of a crumbling courtyard, sunlight catching the silver in her hair. She looked peaceful. It made you furious.

In 2016, Miriam was diagnosed with late-stage ovarian cancer. Her sister, Lila, emailed you: *She doesn’t want visitors, but she asked about you. Said she forgave you.* You deleted the email. A month later, you sent Lila a sympathy card signed *An Admirer of Her Work*. You didn’t sign your name.

When the stroke came in 2023, you were alone in your office at Columbia, reviewing student theses. Your hand froze mid-sentence. You couldn’t speak. The paramedics arrived twenty minutes later. At the hospital, they stabilized you, but the neurologist said there was significant damage. You lay in the ICU, aware but mute, for seventeen days.

On the morning of May 12, your daughter Clara came to visit. She brought her two children, age six and eight. They pressed their hands against the glass of your room, drawing hearts. Clara whispered, “We’re here, Mom. You’re going to be okay.”

You tried to nod.

That afternoon, your body shut down. The monitor flatlined at 3:47 p.m. Clara held your hand as the nurse turned off the machine.

The last thing you heard was her saying Miriam’s name—not yours—when she called the others to tell them you were gone.

prompts.craft_suffix:
Write in the second person — "you," not "she/he/they." Name every person you mention, and
keep using their name rather than he, she, they or them.

Stop at the moment of your death. Do not describe arriving anywhere, and do not describe
the room.

End on a fact, not on what it meant. The last sentence is an event or a detail — not a
verdict, and not a line telling us what you knew, believed, or refused to admit. Leave
that for the others in the room to find out.
